cards.title: Recognizing and constructing mim-width-one decompositions
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, on any finite graph G, either outputs a branch decomposition of mim-width at most one or correctly reports that no such decomposition exists?
cards.why: Would determine whether the especially useful width-one case can be detected and decomposed efficiently, making its decomposition-based algorithms available on arbitrary input graphs.
cards.status_note: Original cut/decomposition definitions and the complete question checked against the ICALP 2026 hardness theorems and open-problems section. No width-one resolution was located through 12 September 2026.

progress.text: The SWAT paper gives algorithms using width-one decompositions and repeats the recognition/construction problem.
ICALP 2026 proves hardness at mim-width two while explicitly preserving the width-one question.

cards.definitions: G=(V,E) is a finite undirected simple graph with n=|V|. For A⊆V, the cut graph G[A,V∖A] keeps exactly those edges with one endpoint in each side; edges internal to either side are discarded. An induced matching in this bipartite graph is a set of vertex-disjoint edges whose endpoints induce exactly those matching edges. Let mim_G(A) be its maximum size. A branch decomposition (T,L) consists of a tree T whose internal nodes have degree three and a bijection L from V to the leaves of T. Deleting a tree edge splits its leaves and hence V into A and V∖A. The decomposition width is the maximum mim_G(A) over its tree-edge cuts. The graph’s mim-width is the minimum over all such decompositions. The target is a decomposition of width ≤1, including width zero for edgeless graphs; empty and one-vertex graphs have the trivial width-zero convention. Runtime is polynomial in the ordinary explicit graph input size. No decomposition or bounded-width promise is supplied. The tree need not be a caterpillar: restricting it to one would instead ask about linear mim-width.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm that returns a valid width-at-most-one decomposition on every yes-instance and rejects every no-instance in polynomial time, or establish an obstruction to this guarantee. Algorithms using a supplied decomposition, recognizing only a subclass, or deciding width at most two do not settle the question.

context_blocks.title: What a width-one cut forbids
context_blocks.text: Across every cut in the chosen tree, there cannot be two disjoint crossing edges with both cross-pair edges absent. Edges inside a side do not affect this test. Equivalently, every cut graph must be a bipartite chain graph.

context_blocks.title: The missing decomposition limits algorithmic use
context_blocks.text: Many graph problems become tractable when a small-mim-width decomposition is available. The source even shows new polynomial-time algorithms at width one, but those guarantees assume the decomposition is supplied.

context_blocks.title: The tree is part of the output
context_blocks.text: Testing the cuts of one given tree is different from finding a tree whose every cut is good. The recognition question must succeed or reject on an arbitrary input graph.

context_blocks.title: The recent hardness result stops at width two
context_blocks.text: The ICALP 2026 paper proves NP-completeness for recognizing mim-width at most two and for width-one recognition of several related parameters. It explicitly leaves ordinary mim-width one open, so those results do not settle this card.

cards.title: A general 3/2 communication lower bound for reliable broadcast
cards.formal: Must every Byzantine reliable-broadcast protocol in the source’s asynchronous authenticated point-to-point model have worst-case large-message communication overhead at least 3/2 asymptotically, when n=3t+1 and up to t parties can be Byzantine, even without a three-round delivery bound or a sublinear-in-n first-round sender load? This selects the source’s version with both restrictions removed.
cards.why: Would settle the leading bandwidth cost of reliable broadcast, a primitive used inside many fault-tolerant distributed protocols.
cards.status_note: Original restrictions and overhead definition checked against MiniCast, the October 2025 full follow-up and the OPODIS 2025 failure-case paper. No general lower-bound resolution was located through 12 September 2026. The question here concerns the unrestricted asynchronous version, not an unrestricted synchronous crash-fault claim.

progress.text: Locher proves a 3/2 lower bound for three-round protocols with restricted first-round sender load and asks to remove these restrictions.
MiniCast provides a general worst-case 3/2 upper bound; subsequent protocols improve latency while retaining that coefficient.
The revised Locher–Shoup follow-up still invokes optimality only under the restricted lower-bound conditions.

references.locator: Full version dated 3 October 2025: abstract and Sections 1–2 read. Gives a three-round bound with the same leading communication coefficient and a two-round signature-based unbalanced variant. Optimality remains tied to the restricted lower bound.

references.locator: OPODIS 2025: abstract, introduction, related work and conclusion read. Still describes the general 3/2 overhead as conjecturally optimal; its 5/3 lower bound imposes an initial full-message broadcast condition.

references.title: Byzantine Reliable Broadcast with Low Communication and Time Complexity
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 15; PDF page 15

cards.definitions: There are n=3t+1 parties with pairwise authenticated channels and a designated sender holding a message m of ℓ bits. Honest-to-honest messages are eventually delivered, with no upper bound on delay; Byzantine parties may deviate arbitrarily. Validity requires every honest party eventually to deliver m when the sender is honest. Agreement requires all honest deliveries to have the same value. Integrity allows each honest party at most one delivery, and totality requires that if one honest party delivers, all honest parties eventually do so. A Byzantine sender may cause no delivery. Let C_A(n,ℓ) be the worst-case total number of bits sent by honest parties in one execution of protocol A, over admissible inputs, faults and delivery schedules. Faulty-party transmissions are not charged. For a faulty sender, the source measures the effective message length by the largest payload fragment an honest party sends under the protocol’s declared encoding. The large-message overhead is L_A(n)=limsup_{ℓ→∞} C_A(n,ℓ)/(nℓ). This uses the upper limit to include protocols without a limiting coefficient; it agrees with the source’s limit whenever that limit exists. The proposed bound is liminf_{t→∞}L_A(3t+1)≥3/2; equivalently, no constant improvement below 3/2 is possible uniformly for all sufficiently large n and sufficiently long messages. The source permits collision-resistant hashing and, for signature-based protocols, signature setup, counting their transmitted bits through a security parameter κ. The payload comparison discards lower-order terms in ℓ, such as O(κn²log n), and uses the source’s cryptographic correctness convention. There is no bound of three on the number of rounds and no restriction that the sender’s first-round total be o(nℓ).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal 3/2 lower bound in the stated unrestricted asynchronous model, or give a correct protocol with a strictly smaller asymptotic worst-case payload coefficient. An upper bound of 3/2 or a lower bound only for three-round, weakly balanced protocols does not resolve this question.

context_blocks.title: The coefficient matters after linear scaling is known
context_blocks.text: Sending an ℓ-bit payload to n parties naturally costs on the order of nℓ bits. The open question concerns the leading constant caused by fault tolerance, rather than whether communication can be linear in payload length.

context_blocks.title: Two restrictions remain in the known lower bound
context_blocks.text: The original theorem applies even to synchronous crash faults, but requires delivery within three rounds and only o(nℓ) first-round bits from the sender. It does not establish the lower bound for protocols that use more rounds or concentrate the load on the sender.

context_blocks.title: Matching upper bounds now exist
context_blocks.text: MiniCast attains leading coefficient 3/2 in the worst case. The later Locher–Shoup work reduces its good-case latency to three rounds and also gives signature-based two-round variants. These constructions strengthen the evidence for optimality but do not prove the general lower bound.

context_blocks.title: Failure-free behavior is not the objective
context_blocks.text: A protocol may use approximately nℓ bits when everything goes well and still need 1.5nℓ bits in its worst execution. The conjecture is about the latter, counting all communication sent by honest parties even when a faulty sender prevents delivery.

cards.context:
Sending an ℓ-bit payload to n parties naturally costs on the order of nℓ bits. The open question concerns the leading constant caused by fault tolerance, rather than whether communication can be linear in payload length.

The original theorem applies even to synchronous crash faults, but requires delivery within three rounds and only o(nℓ) first-round bits from the sender. It does not establish the lower bound for protocols that use more rounds or concentrate the load on the sender.

MiniCast attains leading coefficient 3/2 in the worst case. The later Locher–Shoup work reduces its good-case latency to three rounds and also gives signature-based two-round variants. These constructions strengthen the evidence for optimality but do not prove the general lower bound.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
